LLM auditresponse for thorium-cpu-check.sh:


<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This is a legitimate packaging helper script for the Thorium Browser AUR package. It performs a CPU compatibility check by reading `/proc/cpuinfo` (a safe, standard read-only interface) to determine whether the installed `thorium-browser-bin` package is the optimal build for the system's CPU instruction sets (AVX2/AVX/SSE4 vs the base build). It runs in two modes: `build` mode warns during package building if a more optimized variant exists, and `runtime` mode optionally shows a desktop notification when the browser launches if a better-matching variant is available.

I found no evidence of malicious behavior: there are no network requests (no curl/wget), no downloads, no code execution (no eval, no decoded blobs, no base64), no file writes outside of output streams, and no attempt to exfiltrate data or modify unrelated system files. The script only reads `/proc/cpuinfo`, calls `getconf LONG_BIT` for architecture detection, and conditionally runs `notify-send` — the latter is properly guarded by checking for an active `DISPLAY` or `WAYLAND_DISPLAY`, so it cannot break headless builds.

Minor notes (hygiene, not malice): the `THORIUM_PACKAGING_SERVER` environment variable bypass exists in build mode so build farms on different hardware can skip the CPU check — this is a standard maintainership pattern and a legitimate convenience, not a backdoor. The runtime notification could be seen as slightly intrusive but is clearly intended to help users switch to a faster-performing package variant, and it does not execute the browser or install anything.
</details>
